iv: Mass of a stack of coffee filters
physics: At terminal velocity weight = drag. If drag ∝ v², then v² ∝ m: plot v² against m.
note: Film the fall and measure speed over the last part, or time a long drop.

iv: Canopy area of a paper parachute
physics: With drag ∝ Av², v² ∝ 1/A for a fixed load: plot v² against 1/A.

iv: Ramp angle
physics: a = g sin θ, minus friction effects: plot a against sin θ; the gradient should be close to g.

iv: Release height of a toy car on a ramp
dv: Distance it rolls along the floor
physics: Energy: mgh = F·d, so d ∝ h if the resistive force is constant. The gradient tells you about the resistive force.

iv: Drop height of a ball
physics: Coefficient of restitution e = √(h_bounce / h_drop): plot h_bounce against h_drop; gradient = e².

iv: Temperature of a tennis or squash ball
physics: No simple equation: find the pattern and compare with published data on ball temperature and bounce.
note: Warm or cool balls in water; the temperature changes quickly once out, so be fast and consistent.

iv: Air pressure inside a ball
physics: Find how e depends on pressure; compare with published sports-science values.
note: Needs a pump with a pressure gauge.

iv: Load hung on the end of a clamped ruler (cantilever)
physics: Beam theory: d = FL³/(3EI), so d ∝ F. The gradient gives Young’s modulus of the ruler.

iv: Overhanging length of a clamped ruler
dv: Deflection of the end under a fixed load
physics: d ∝ L³: plot ln d against ln L and check the gradient is about 3.

iv: Overhanging length of a clamped ruler with a mass on the end
physics: Stiffness k ∝ 1/L³, so T ∝ L^1.5 when the end mass dominates: plot ln T against ln L.

iv: Span of a ruler supported at both ends
dv: Sag at the middle under a fixed load
physics: d = FL³/(48EI), so d ∝ L³ (log–log gradient 3).

iv: Drop height of a ball bearing
dv: Diameter of the crater in sand or flour
physics: Crater size grows as a power of the impact energy: find the power from a ln–ln graph and compare with published studies.

iv: Diameter of a funnel’s opening
dv: Time for sand or rice to drain out
physics: Beverloo’s law: flow rate ∝ D^2.5, so the time for a fixed amount ∝ D^−2.5.

iv: Release angle of a pendulum
physics: The small-angle formula breaks down: T ≈ T₀(1 + θ₀²/16) with θ₀ in radians, so plot T against θ₀².

iv: Length of a pendulum
physics: T = 2π√(L/g): plot T² against L; gradient = 4π²/g.
note: A classic: fine if your analysis and evaluation are strong.

iv: Mass on a spring
physics: T = 2π√(m/k): plot T² against m; the gradient gives k, and the intercept shows the spring’s own mass.

iv: Separation of the two strings of a bifilar pendulum
physics: T ∝ 1/d: plot T against 1/d.

iv: Number of coils of a hanging slinky
physics: Stiffness ∝ 1/N and mass ∝ N, so T ∝ N.

iv: Radius of a ball rolling inside a large curved bowl
physics: Rolling without slipping: T = 2π√(7(R − r)/(5g)), so T² ∝ (R − r).

iv: Area of a card attached to an oscillating mass on a spring
dv: Amplitude after a set number of oscillations (damping)
physics: Amplitude decays exponentially; the decay rate increases with area. Find the relationship.

iv: Temperature difference between hot water and the room
physics: Newton’s law of cooling: rate ∝ (T − T_room). Plot rate against ΔT, or ln ΔT against time.

iv: Volume of water in a cup
physics: Heat loss depends on surface area and heat capacity depends on mass, so the rate falls as volume rises. Find the relationship.

iv: Thickness of insulation (layers) around a container
physics: Conduction: rate of heat loss falls as thickness rises (roughly ∝ 1/thickness for thin layers).

iv: Temperature of a viscous liquid (honey, oil, syrup)
dv: Time for a ball to fall a fixed distance through it
physics: Stokes’ law: fall speed ∝ 1/viscosity. Viscosity drops sharply as temperature rises; try ln t against 1/T (T in kelvin).
note: Use a tall column so fall times are several seconds.

iv: Vibrating length of a string
physics: f = (1/2L)√(F/μ): plot f against 1/L; gradient = v/2.
note: A phone frequency app measures f.

iv: Tension in a string
physics: f ∝ √F: plot f² against F; the gradient gives the mass per length.

iv: Volume of water in a wine glass
physics: No simple textbook equation: find the pattern, then compare with published studies of wine-glass resonance.

iv: Length of the air column in a tube partly filled with water
physics: Closed pipe: f = v/(4(L + e)). Plot 1/f against L: the gradient gives the speed of sound, the intercept the end correction e.

iv: Distance from a speaker
physics: Inverse square law: the level should drop about 6 dB per doubling of distance. Plot dB against log r.
note: Work outdoors or in a large room; reflections spoil it.

iv: Distance from a small bulb
physics: Inverse square law for a point source: I ∝ 1/r². Plot I against 1/r², or ln I against ln r (gradient −2).
note: Use a phone light-sensor app in a dark room.

iv: Angle between two polarising filters
physics: Malus’s law: I = I₀ cos²θ. Plot I against cos²θ.

iv: Number of sheets of plastic or glass
physics: Each sheet removes the same fraction: I = I₀e^(−kn). Plot ln I against n.

iv: Distance from a hair (or slit) to the screen
dv: Width of the central bright band
physics: Diffraction: width ≈ 2λD/b. The gradient gives the hair’s thickness b.
note: Laser pointer: never point it at eyes. Ask before using one.

iv: Temperature of a small solar cell
physics: A solar cell’s voltage falls roughly linearly as it warms. Compare the gradient with the manufacturer’s temperature coefficient.

iv: Colour (wavelength) of an LED
dv: Voltage at which it starts to glow
physics: eV ≈ hc/λ: plot V against 1/λ; the gradient gives an estimate of Planck’s constant.

iv: Distance from a magnet
physics: Far from the magnet, B ∝ 1/r³ along its axis: plot ln B against ln r (gradient −3).
note: A phone magnetometer app measures B. Subtract the background (Earth’s) field.

iv: Current in a coil
physics: B ∝ I for a coil (B = μ₀nI for a long solenoid). The gradient leads to μ₀.

iv: Temperature of a magnet
physics: Permanent magnets weaken as they warm. Find the relationship and compare with published temperature coefficients.

iv: Wall thickness (or material) of a copper or aluminium pipe
dv: Time for a strong magnet to fall through it
physics: Eddy currents: the slowing force grows with wall thickness and conductivity, so the fall time rises with both.
note: Fall times of several seconds make hand timing workable.

iv: Resistance in an RC circuit
dv: Time for the capacitor’s voltage to halve
physics: t½ = RC ln 2: plot t½ against R; the gradient gives the capacitance.
note: Large capacitors make times long enough to read a multimeter.

iv: Temperature of a battery
physics: From V = ε − Ir at each temperature: find r from a V–I graph, then plot r against temperature.

iv: Height a magnet falls through a coil
physics: Faraday’s law: a faster magnet gives a bigger emf, and speed ∝ √h, so expect the peak emf ∝ √h.
note: Needs a data logger fast enough to catch the peak.

iv: Time since a bottle started draining through a small hole
physics: Torricelli: √h falls linearly with time. Plot √h against t.

iv: Inner diameter of a siphon tube
physics: Flow rises steeply with diameter. Find the power from a ln–ln graph and compare with Poiseuille’s law (∝ d⁴) for slow, smooth flow.

iv: Drop height of a water droplet
dv: Rebound height from a water surface
physics: Find the pattern with slow-motion video; compare with published droplet studies.
